## Goal: Wrangle and interact with a variety of data types {.smaller}


Requires expanding our understanding of **data structures** in `R`.


::: {.nonincremental}

* Most common data structure = `data.frame`/data set/spreadsheet

* Example: Portland Biketown bike rental data.

:::

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
biketown <- read_csv("data/biketown.csv")
biketown %>%
  select(BikeID, Duration, PaymentPlan, StartTime, EndTime) %>%
  as.data.frame()
```

## Other Data Structures: Spatial Data Frames {.small}

::: {.nonincremental}

- From **points** to **polyons** to **rasters**, and more! We learned how to interact with spatial data in `R`!

:::

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.width= 6}

api_key <- "ff47b8f510c3db70501a7463b61e1298db1db97d"

library(tidycensus)
options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)
or <- get_acs(state = "OR",  geography = "county", 
                  variables = "B19013_001", geometry = TRUE, 
              key = api_key) 
options(scipen = 999)
ggplot(data = or, mapping = aes(geometry = geometry,
                                fill = estimate)) + 
  geom_sf() +
  coord_sf() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() + theme_void()
```


![](img/sf.gif){width="13%" style="float:left; padding:25px"}

![](img/terra.png){width="13%" style="float:right; padding:25px"}


<br> 
<br>

::: {.nonincremental}

* We used `sf` and `terra` to interact with spatial data

:::

# Learning Goals: Data Viz

## Goal: Create **static** data visualizations of multivariate data with `ggplot2`

![](img/ggplot2.png){width="10%" style="float:left; padding:25px"}

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.width= 9, fig.asp= .6}
library(babynames)
babynames_stat108 <- babynames %>%
  filter(name %in% c("Grayson", "Michael", "Megan",
                     "Lenny")) %>%
  group_by(year, name) %>%
  summarize(n = sum(n))

p <- ggplot(data = babynames_stat108, 
       mapping = aes(x = year, y = n)) +
  geom_line(aes(color = name), size = 2) + 
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", text = element_text(size=20)) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  labs(y = "Number of Births", x = "Year", color = "Baby Name")
p
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Goal: Create **animated** data visualizations of multivariate data with `gganimate`

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.width= 9, fig.asp= .6}
library(gganimate)
p_animate <- p +
  transition_reveal(along = year)
animate(p_animate, fps = 5, end_pause = 20, height = 4,
  width = 6.5, units = "in", res = 100)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Goal: Create **interactive** data visualizations of multivariate data with `plotly` and `shiny`

![](img/plotlyshiny.001.jpeg){width="30%" style="float:left; padding:25px"}

```{r, echo= FALSE}
library(plotly)
ggplotly(p)
```

# Creating a Quarto website

Inspired by Charlotte Wickham's talk: *From Zero to Website in 20 Minutes*

------------------------------------------------------------------------


## Step 1: Create another `r emo::ji("sparkles")` special `r emo::ji("sparkles")` repo


![](img/maurvie-git-website.png){width='75%' fig-align='center'}



------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Step 2: Grab a basic template to get you started

After cloning your repo, run the following in terminal:

<br>

``` 
quarto use template cwickham/minimal-website
```

<br>

Important files created:

- `_quarto.yml`: control important site metadata and (some) formatting
- `index.qmd`: generates your site's landing page


------------------------------------------------------------------------


## Step 3: Make some important changes

In `_quarto.yml`: 

::: {.fragment .nonincremental}

- Specify correct output directory: 

```
project:
  type: website
  output-dir: docs
```

:::


<br>

In `index.qmd`: 

- Add some of your information and then press `Render`!

- Play around with `template:`. Options built in are jolla, trestles, solana, marquee, and broadside


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Step 4: Admire


![](img/maurvie-website.png){width='75%' fig-align='center'}


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Step 5: Commit and push!


![](img/maurvie-pushed.png){width='75%' fig-align='center'}


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Step 6: Set up GitHub Pages

- In your repo, go to "Settings" and then, under the "Code and automation" subheader select "Pages"

- Change `Branch: None` to `Branch: main`, and `/ (root)` to `/docs`. Press `Save`.

- Navigate back to the GitHub repo page. You should see the following:

------------------------------------------------------------------------


## Step 6: Set up GitHub Pages



![](img/maurvie-deployed.png){width='75%' fig-align='center'}



------------------------------------------------------------------------

- [https://maurvieee.github.io/](https://maurvieee.github.io/)

## Success!


:::: {.columns}


::: {.column}


- Your website is now hosted publicly thanks to Quarto and GitHub Pages!

- It's now time to add more pages, all the info you'd like to share, and to customize the aesthetics of your page!

- As long as you press "Render" from `index.qmd` before you push, your website will automatically update through the GitHub Action that was created when we set up GitHub Pages. 


:::

::: {.column}

![](img/lemurs.png){width="100%" fig-align='center'}

:::

::::

## Adding pages 


- Each page of your website will be a `.qmd` file.

- To add a new page, create a new `.qmd` file!

- [My website](https://graysonwhite.com/) has [relatively simple pages](https://graysonwhite.com/teaching.html) throughout

## Listings 

- There are a few ways to set these up, but I prefer to: 
    - Create a **folder** where each "listing" (one `.qmd` file for each listing) will live, and
    - Create a `.qmd` **file** in the **main directory** that points to that folder. 


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Listings 

- Now, put some blog posts (`.qmd` files) in the `posts` directory

- Setting the `date` in the YAML of each blog posts orders them. 

- Don't forget to add navigation to the `blog.qmd` page so your users can find your blog.


------------------------------------------------------------------------


## Listings 

![](img/maurvie-lemur-source.png){width='50%' fig-align='center'}

- You don't need to update `blog.qmd`, it will automatically populate when you add listings in the `posts` folder.



------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Listings 

Render your site and admire!

![](img/maurvie-blog.png){width='65%' fig-align='center'}


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Listings 

- Lots of customization options [here](https://quarto.org/docs/websites/website-listings.html)
    - Setting `type:` to `default`, `table`, or `grid` changes how your blog posts appear. 
    
- Can also give a custom list of items to go in listings, rather than all the posts in a folder
    - Can set this up with a YAML file. See [Charlotte's slides](https://charlotte.quarto.pub/jsm2024/#/contents-can-be-a-yaml-file)

## Custom themes

::: {.nonincremental}

- There are a [ton of themes](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-themes.html) to pick from!
    - Set the theme in your `_quarto.yml` file
    - (Default theme: cosmo + your custom `.scss`)
    - Let's swap out cosmo for some other themes!
    
- The following screenshots removed the custom `.scss` to show fully what the theme changes. Our `custom.scss` overwrites some theme elements.
    
:::

## Total customization with `styles.scss`

- Gives you the ability to overwrite elements of your chosen theme

- Allows you to edit things like **font** and **color**



------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Total customization with `styles.scss`

------------------------------------------------------------------------


## Total customization with `styles.scss`


When you've found the font you'd like to add, import the font by Clicking "Get Font" and then "Get Embed Code". 

::: {.fragment}

Then, copy the code with `@import`: 


![](img/import-font.png){width='50%' fig-align='center'}

:::






------------------------------------------------------------------------


## Total customization with `styles.scss`


Paste

```
@import url('https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Libre+Baskerville:ital,wght@0,400..700;1,400..700&display=swap');
```

into `styles.scss`.

I am just scratching the surface when it comes to customizing your website. 

Some of my favorite resources for Quarto website customization: 

- [The Quarto.org HTML Themes Documentation](https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/html-themes.html)

- For a **deep dive** into customization, see [Sam Shanny-Csik](https://samanthacsik.github.io/)'s slides on [Customizing Quarto Websites](https://ucsb-meds.github.io/customizing-quarto-websites/#/title-slide)
